name: Deep Champagne
lede: Deep Champagne is a pale, warm orange-yellow named for the wine, a CSS keyword also carried by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955, and the first-seen match in our archive goes back to the year 1000.

sections.title: Named for the wine
sections.body:
Our data traces the name to champagne, the sparkling wine, a plant-and-landscape word rather than a pigment [1]. It is a CSS color keyword, and Wikipedia's entry for it cites the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, which files the hue as block 73, "pale orange yellow" [1]. That single ISCC-NBS block holds dozens of other names besides Deep Champagne, among them Almond Cream, Apricot Cream and Bath Stone, which gives a sense of how finely that one pale tan region has been subdivided by different namers over time [1].

Its nearest distinct neighbor by computed color distance is [[leghorn|Leghorn]], 3.4 units away and read in our data as "darker" [2]. [[wheat|Wheat]] sits a touch further, 4.2 units off, called "duller" [2]. In LCH terms Deep Champagne measures lightness 88, chroma 29, hue 79 degrees: light, moderately saturated, and warm [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a close match covers enough of the canvas in 566, as photographed, more common than 76 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1400s, at 1.2 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Pierre Puvis de Chavannes is its most devoted painter here, with the color present in 4 of 25 of his works, well above the baseline of the museums those works come from [3]. Its earliest archive match is a painting dated to the year 1000, nine centuries before champagne itself existed as a sparkling wine; the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not evidence of the drink or the name [3].
